newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices fall despite cut in Nigerian output.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices fall despite cut in Nigerian output.

text.p: Oil prices fell on Monday as sluggish demand for physical barrels eclipsed the potentially bullish loss of some Nigerian crude oil output, dealers said.
They attributed crude oil's weakness to a relative lack of buying interest for crude oil in the key refining regions of Singapore, the United States and Northwest Europe.
London futures for North Sea benchmark Brent blend closed 40 cents down at $19.58 a barrel.
Sluggish fundamentals discouraged any knee-jerk reactions to the Nigerian news among futures traders.
"It may be difficult to look for a recovery in oil prices until we're able to clear out the physical overhang we're seeing in North Sea markets," said Smith Barney analyst Mari Buglass.
"One might have expected some notional support from the Nigeria news to buoy futures prices, but we really haven't seen it," Buglass added.

Anglo-Dutch oil giant Royal Dutch/Shell said on Monday it had been dragged into a dispute between villagers in Nigeria's oil rich Niger Delta region and 126 of its staff and contractors, all Nigerians, had been detained.
Villagers on Monday agreed to release six of the detained staff who had been injured, Shell said.

The occupation of six pumping stations in the oil-rich region by villagers forced Shell to shut in some 100,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil production, equivalent to about 10 percent of its Nigerian output.
Shell said exports and deliveries to refineries in Nigeria had not been affected and would continue as normal for the foreseeable future.
"This will not affect exports for the remainder of this month," a Shell official said.
Nigeria, with a crude oil output of about 2.15 million bpd, is the fifth biggest producer in the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC). Shell pumps about half.

Brokers attributed Monday's sliding oil price to a growing congregation of unsold cargoes in the North Sea as seasonal refinery maintenance curtailed regional crude needs and transatlantic trade opportunities failed to provide a viable outlet.

European markets continued to look to the U.S. gasoline market for support, but questions surrounding the demand forecast for the all-important U.S. driving season left traders on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) less than exuberant about short-term prospects.
"U.S. gasoline has been looming in the wings for a while. The question is when it will kick in to lend support," said one trader.
